lead: The blue-team analyst cert. It proves you can work a SOC: spot malicious activity, run vulnerability management, respond to incidents and report what happened. The natural next step after Security+.

v4.label: V4
v4.note: The new version. Adds AI in security operations and more identity and cloud detection. Pick this if you'll test after December 22, 2026.
v4.onote: Listed in the order of CompTIA's V4 objectives summary. Official numbering is in the V4 objectives PDF.

domains.name: Security Operations
obj: Explain system and network architecture concepts in security operations
Security architecture components, identity concepts and logging practices.
Analyze indicators of potential malicious activity
Suspicious activity across networks, endpoints, cloud and identity systems.
Use tools to determine malicious activity
SIEM, EDR, packet analysis tools and threat intelligence platforms.
Explain threat intelligence and threat-hunting concepts
Frameworks, data sources and methods to identify and investigate threats.
Describe efficiency and process improvement in security operations
Automation, workflows and processes that make a SOC run better.
Summarize concepts related to the use of AI in security operations
Use cases, risks and governance considerations.

domains.name: Vulnerability Management
obj: Implement the appropriate vulnerability scanning method
Tools and techniques to find vulnerabilities in systems, networks and applications.
Analyze output from vulnerability assessment tools
Vulnerabilities, findings and security gaps in scan results.
Prioritize and mitigate vulnerabilities
Risk-based approaches using scoring systems, threat intelligence and business context.
Explain concepts related to control types, risks, and vulnerability management
Controls, policies and compliance practices for managing risk.

domains.name: Incident Response and Management
obj: Summarize concepts related to attack methodology frameworks
Models such as MITRE ATT&CK and the Cyber Kill Chain.
Outline the incident response process
Preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication and recovery.
Implement incident response techniques
Triage, evidence handling, escalation, remediation and root cause identification.

domains.name: Reporting and Communication
obj: Explain vulnerability management reporting and communication
Reports, dashboards and communication that present findings and support escalation.
Describe security operations, incident response reporting, and communication
Incident documentation, post-incident reviews, and metrics like detection time, response time and remediation effectiveness.

v3.label: V3
v3.note: The outgoing version. CompTIA stops selling its official English study material on November 22, 2026, and the English exam retires December 22, 2026 (Japanese, Portuguese and Spanish run until March 23, 2027). Only pick it if you can test before then. Both versions earn the same CySA+.

domains.name: Security Operations
obj: Explain the importance of system and network architecture concepts in security operations
Logging, OS concepts, infrastructure, IAM, encryption, sensitive data protection.
Given a scenario, analyze indicators of potentially malicious activity
Network, host, application and other indicators: beaconing, unusual traffic, processes, registry changes.
Given a scenario, use appropriate tools or techniques to determine malicious activity
SIEM, EDR, packet capture, DNS and IP reputation, file analysis, sandboxing, basic scripting.
Compare and contrast threat-intelligence and threat-hunting concepts
Threat actors, TTPs, confidence levels, collection sources, intel sharing, hunting.
Explain the importance of efficiency and process improvement in security operations
Standardized processes, automation, SOAR, technology integration, single pane of glass.

domains.name: Vulnerability Management
obj: Given a scenario, implement vulnerability scanning methods and concepts
Asset discovery, internal vs external, credentialed vs non-credentialed, agent vs agentless, active vs passive.
Given a scenario, analyze output from vulnerability assessment tools
Network scanners, web app scanners, vulnerability scanners, debuggers, cloud tools.
Given a scenario, analyze data to prioritize vulnerabilities
CVSS, validation, context, exploitability, asset value, zero-days.
Given a scenario, recommend controls to mitigate attacks and software vulnerabilities
XSS, overflows, injection, broken access control, SSRF, insecure configuration.
Explain concepts related to vulnerability response, handling, and management
Compensating controls, patching, maintenance windows, exceptions, risk management, SDLC.

domains.name: Incident Response and Management
obj: Explain concepts related to attack methodology frameworks
Cyber Kill Chain, Diamond Model, MITRE ATT&CK, OSSTMM, OWASP Testing Guide.
Given a scenario, perform incident response activities
Detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, evidence and chain of custody.
Explain the preparation and post-incident activity phases of the incident management life cycle
IR plans, tools, playbooks, training, testing, lessons learned, root cause analysis.

domains.name: Reporting and Communication
obj: Explain the importance of vulnerability management reporting and communication
Vulnerability reports, compliance reports, action plans, inhibitors to remediation, metrics.
Explain the importance of incident response reporting and communication
Stakeholders, incident declaration and escalation, reports, communications, root cause, metrics.

extras.title: Incident response phases
rows: Plans, playbooks, tools, training and contacts, before anything happens.
Alerts, reports and hunts that surface a possible incident.
Confirm it's real, scope it, set severity, start the timeline.
Stop the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block indicators.
Remove the attacker: malware, persistence, rogue accounts.
Restore and monitor systems, return to normal operations.
Lessons learned, root cause, improve detections and the plan.

extras.title: SOC metrics
rows: Start of an incident until the SOC notices it.
Detection until the threat is handled.
How long the attacker was inside before being found.
Share of alerts that weren't real. Drives tuning work.
Agreed time to act on a finding, often by severity.

extras.title: Reading a CVSS vector
extras.sub: 2.0 · CVSS 3.1 base metrics, still the most common in scan reports
rows: N network · A adjacent · L local · P physical. Network is the easiest to reach.
L low · H high. Low means the attack works reliably.
N none · L low · H high. None means no login is needed.
N none · R required. None means no one has to click anything.
U unchanged · C changed. Changed means it can break out to other components.
H high · L low · N none, for confidentiality, integrity and availability.

method: Use the domains above as your checklist. Security Operations alone is a third of the exam.
Learn the analyst workflow, not just terms: alert, triage, investigate, contain, report.
Work real SOC labs: SIEM searches, EDR alerts, packet captures, phishing analysis. Blue-team lab sites are free.
Flashcards for IR phases, CVSS metrics, Windows event IDs, common ports and attack frameworks.
165 minutes is long. Take full-length timed practice exams to build stamina, and review every miss.
tips: They often come first and are log-heavy. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.
165 minutes for up to 85 questions gives you almost 2 minutes each. Use it to read the logs carefully.
When asked what to do FIRST, it's usually confirm or contain before you eradicate.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

Investigation challenges built on real logs and packet captures.

Vulnerabilities being exploited right now. The key input for prioritizing.

quiz.q: A workstation makes an outbound HTTPS connection to the same external IP every 60 seconds (±2 s), sending about 300 bytes each time, all night while the user is logged off. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: Command-and-control beaconing
Right. Regular intervals with small, consistent payloads and no user present is the classic beacon pattern. Jitter of a couple of seconds is common.
Data exfiltration
Exfiltration moves large or growing volumes of data. 300 bytes a minute is a heartbeat, not a transfer.
DNS tunneling
Tunneling shows up as many DNS queries with long, random-looking subdomains, not HTTPS to one IP.
A port scan
A scan hits many ports or hosts in a short burst, not one destination on a steady timer.

quiz.q: Which Windows Security event is the BEST evidence that a pass-the-hash attempt SUCCEEDED against a file server?
o: 4624, logon type 3, using NTLM, from an unexpected workstation
Right. 4624 is a successful logon; type 3 is network; NTLM plus an odd source is the pass-the-hash signature.
4625, failed logon
4625 records failures. The question asks for evidence the attempt worked.
4688, new process created
Process creation can show what ran afterwards, but not how the attacker authenticated.
4720, user account created
Account creation could be later persistence. It isn't evidence of the logon technique.

quiz.q: A SOC wants detections that cost an attacker the MOST effort to get around. Which should it build?
o: A behavior-based alert for any process reading LSASS memory
Right. Detecting the technique (a TTP) sits at the top of the Pyramid of Pain. The attacker has to change how they operate.
A blocklist of known malware file hashes
Hashes are trivial to change. Recompiling or one changed byte beats it.
A blocklist of known attacker IP addresses
IPs are cheap to rotate through VPNs, proxies or new cloud hosts.
A blocklist of known C2 domains
Domains take a little more effort than IPs, but new ones can be registered in minutes.

quiz.q: A SOC is adding an AI assistant that can close alerts and isolate hosts on its own. Which control BEST addresses the governance risk?
o: Require analyst approval before the AI isolates hosts or closes high-severity alerts
Right. A human in the loop for high-impact actions limits the damage from wrong or manipulated AI decisions.
Let the AI close every alert it rates as low confidence
Low-confidence calls are exactly the ones that most need a human to look.
Turn off logging of AI decisions to save storage
Without an audit trail you can't review, tune or explain what the AI did.
Give the AI domain admin rights so it never fails an action
That breaks least privilege. A misled AI with admin rights is a disaster.

quiz.q: A vulnerability scan reports far fewer missing patches on Windows servers than the patch management system shows. What is the MOST likely reason?
o: The scan was non-credentialed, so it couldn't see installed software
Right. Without a login, the scanner only sees what's exposed on the network. Credentialed scans read installed versions and patch levels.
The scanner's plugins are too new
Newer plugins find more issues, not fewer.
The servers were scanned during business hours
Timing doesn't hide missing patches.
The patch system is reporting false positives
Possible, but the far more common cause of this gap is a scan without credentials.

quiz.q: Which vulnerability should be remediated FIRST?
o: CVSS 7.5 on an internet-facing VPN appliance, listed in CISA's KEV catalog
Right. It's reachable from the internet and is being exploited in the wild right now. Real-world risk beats a raw score.
CVSS 9.8 on an isolated lab server with no network path in
High score, but almost no exposure, so the actual risk is low.
CVSS 8.1 on an internal app that requires an authenticated admin to exploit
Needing admin access and internal reach makes this much harder to exploit.
CVSS 5.3 information disclosure on the intranet homepage
Low severity and internal. It belongs later in the queue.

quiz.q: A scan report shows CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. What does this vector mean?
o: Remotely exploitable with no login and no user action, with full impact to confidentiality, integrity and availability
Right. Network vector, low complexity, no privileges, no interaction, high C/I/A. This is a critical 9.8.
Exploitable only with physical access, but with high impact
AV:N means network, not physical (AV:P).
Requires a user to click a link, then affects only availability
UI:N means no interaction is needed, and C and I are high too, not just A.
Needs an admin account, and the impact spreads to other systems
PR:N means no privileges are needed, and S:U means scope is unchanged.

quiz.q: After containing a breach, the team deletes a malicious scheduled task, removes a rogue admin account and reimages two workstations. Which incident response phase is this?
o: Eradication
Right. Removing the attacker's footholds and malware is eradication.
Containment
Containment stops the spread, like isolating hosts. That was already done.
Recovery
Recovery comes next: restoring service and monitoring that the systems stay clean.
Post-incident activity
Lessons learned and root cause happen after recovery.

quiz.q: An attacker emails a user a document with a malicious macro. On the Cyber Kill Chain, which stage is the email itself?
o: Delivery
Right. Delivery is getting the weapon to the target: here, the phishing email.
Weaponization
Weaponization is building the malicious document, before it's sent.
Exploitation
Exploitation is the macro actually running when the user opens the file.
Installation
Installation is when malware sets up persistence on the host.

quiz.q: Leadership wants a metric for the average time from when an incident begins until the SOC detects it. Which metric is this?
o: Mean time to detect (MTTD)
Right. MTTD measures how long threats go unnoticed. Lower is better.
Mean time to respond (MTTR)
MTTR starts at detection and measures how quickly the threat is handled.
Service level agreement (SLA)
An SLA is a target or promise, not a measured average.
False positive rate
That measures alert quality, not speed.

pbqs.title: Fix the vulnerability scan findings
pbqs.scenario: Your weekly scan flagged six findings. Read each one and pick the BEST remediation. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.
choices: Set Secure and HttpOnly on the cookie
Verify, then mark as a false positive

items.log:
Plugin 104743  TLS Version 1.0 Protocol Detection  Medium
The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.
items.why: Old TLS versions have known weaknesses. Turn them off and allow only TLS 1.2 and 1.3.

items.log:
Plugin 96982  Server Message Block (SMB) Protocol Version 1 Enabled  Medium
SMBv1 is deprecated; EternalBlue-class exploits target it.
items.why: SMBv1 is obsolete and was the path for WannaCry. Disable it; modern Windows uses SMBv2/3.

items.log: Plugin 11219  Web interface accepts default credentials (admin / admin)  High
items.why: Default credentials are public knowledge. Change them (and restrict the admin page).

items.log:
Plugin 153584  Apache 2.4.49 < 2.4.51 Path Traversal (CVE-2021-41773)  Critical
Listed in CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities.
items.why: A known, actively exploited bug in the software version itself. The only real fix is upgrading Apache.

items.log:
Plugin 112529  Session cookie without Secure/HttpOnly flags  Low
Set-Cookie: SESSIONID=8f3a...; Path=/
items.why: Secure keeps the cookie on HTTPS only; HttpOnly keeps scripts from stealing it.

items.log:
Plugin 10671  Microsoft IIS 6.0 WebDAV Remote Code Execution  Critical
Host OS: Ubuntu 24.04 · Server header: nginx/1.24.0
items.why: An IIS finding on a Linux host running nginx doesn't fit. Confirm it, then document it as a false positive instead of patching nothing.

pbqs.title: Triage the SIEM queue
pbqs.scenario: You're on shift and four alerts are in the queue. Decide whether each one is malicious or benign, and pick the right next step. Each next step is used once.

rows.req: Impossible travel: j.ortiz signs in from Virginia, then from overseas 9 minutes later. An MFA push was approved, and a new inbox rule forwards all mail to an outside address.
rows.why: An approved MFA push plus a forwarding rule means the account is taken over. Disable it and revoke active sessions so stolen tokens stop working.

rows.req: EDR: WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe -enc JABzAD0A…, which then connected to a domain registered yesterday.
rows.why: Office launching encoded PowerShell that calls a brand-new domain is a classic malicious macro. Isolate the host before it spreads.

rows.req: Port scan detected from 10.10.5.20, the vulnerability scanner, during the approved Tuesday scan window.
rows.why: A real scan, but authorized. Close it and tune the rule to exclude the scanner during its window so it stops wasting analyst time.

rows.req: Antivirus caught the EICAR test file on a help desk laptop. Ticket #8812 says IT is testing AV coverage today.
rows.why: EICAR is a harmless test file and the activity is approved. Close it and note the ticket so the record shows why.
